prompt: Which thalamic nucleus relays touch from the body versus the face?
explain: Somatotopy in the thalamus: the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) receives the medial lemniscus from the body, while the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) receives trigeminal input from the face.

source.ref: lecture-9, Sensory Pathway Cheat Sheet extended

prompt: Where does VPM project?
answer: Primary somatosensory cortex (face area), via the internal capsule

prompt: Which sensations are relayed by the spinal trigeminal nucleus?
answer: Pain, temperature, itch and crude touch

prompt: Which cranial nerves send pain/temperature input to the spinal trigeminal nucleus?
explain: Besides V, the facial (VII), glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves carry somatic sensation from the ear and pharynx; their pain and temperature fibers also descend into the spinal trigeminal tract and end in the spinal trigeminal nucleus.

prompt: Where is the second-order neuron for facial pain and temperature?
answer: Spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve

prompt: The spinal trigeminal nucleus is largest at which level?
answer: Caudal medulla (a long column from pons to upper cervical cord)

prompt: Which tract carries second-order facial pain fibers to the thalamus?
Which thalamic nucleus relays facial pain and temperature?
Facial pain and temperature fibers run next to which body pathway in the brainstem?
A lesion of the right spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract in the lateral medulla causes loss of facial pain on which side?
answer: Right (ipsilateral): fibers cross after the nucleus
explain: First-order pain fibers descend ipsilaterally in the spinal trigeminal tract and synapse in the ipsilateral spinal trigeminal nucleus; second-order axons cross afterward. A lesion of the nucleus/tract in the lateral medulla (as in lateral medullary syndrome) therefore causes ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss.

prompt: A lesion of the right trigeminothalamic tract (after crossing) causes facial pain loss on which side?
explain: After the second-order axons cross, the trigeminothalamic tract carries information from the opposite face, so a right-sided lesion there causes left facial pain and temperature loss.

prompt: Where are the cell bodies of mesencephalic V neurons, unlike other primary sensory neurons?
answer: Inside the brainstem, in the mesencephalic nucleus (not in a ganglion)

prompt: Mesencephalic V axons synapse monosynaptically on which nucleus?
What is the purpose of the mesencephalic nucleus?
answer: Jaw reflex: proprioception from muscles of mastication (prevents biting too hard)

prompt: Where do lateral corticospinal tract neurons have their cell bodies?
answer: Layer V of primary motor cortex (and premotor/sensory areas)

prompt: Name the white-matter route of corticospinal axons from cortex to medulla.
answer: Corona radiata, internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, longitudinal fibers of the pons, pyramid
explain: Corticospinal axons descend through the corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), longitudinal fibers of the pons and medullary pyramid, then cross at the motor decussation into the lateral corticospinal tract.

prompt: Through which part of the internal capsule do cortical efferents (corticospinal/corticobulbar) descend?
explain: Corticobulbar fibres run in the genu and corticospinal fibres in the posterior limb (StatPearls; DTI places the CST in the posterior part of the posterior limb). Lecture 10 slide 12's 'anterior limb and genu' is being corrected.

prompt: In which midbrain structure do cortical efferents travel?
In which pontine structure do corticospinal fibers travel?
In which medullary structure do corticospinal fibers travel?
Where does the lateral corticospinal tract decussate?
What percentage of corticospinal fibers cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract?
In which funiculus does the lateral corticospinal tract travel?
Where does the lateral corticospinal tract terminate?
answer: Lateral ventral horn motor neuron pools for limb muscles, ipsilateral to the tract

prompt: What movements does the lateral corticospinal tract control?
answer: Voluntary movement of distal limb muscles

prompt: A lesion of the right lateral corticospinal tract in the cervical cord causes spastic weakness on which side?
answer: Right (ipsilateral): the tract has already crossed
explain: The lateral corticospinal tract crosses in the medulla (motor decussation), so a cord lesion below that level affects the muscles on the same side as the lesion.

prompt: A stroke in the right internal capsule produces weakness on which side of the body?
explain: The corticospinal tract is still uncrossed in the internal capsule and crosses lower in the medulla, so a right capsule stroke causes left-sided weakness.

prompt: A lesion of the left pyramid (above the decussation) causes weakness on which side?
explain: The pyramid carries uncrossed fibers above the motor decussation, so a left pyramid lesion causes right-sided weakness.

prompt: Name signs of an upper motor neuron lesion in the corticospinal tract.
answer: Spastic paralysis (rigidity), Babinski sign, no atrophy

prompt: Anterior corticospinal fibers arise from which fraction of pyramidal fibers?
answer: The ~20% that do not cross in the medulla

prompt: In which funiculus does the anterior corticospinal tract travel?
Where does the anterior corticospinal tract terminate?
answer: Medial ventral horn motor pools of axial (trunk) muscles, bilaterally

prompt: What does the anterior corticospinal tract control?
answer: Voluntary axial (trunk) and proximal limb muscles, bilaterally

prompt: True or false: the anterior corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla.
explain: It stays uncrossed and terminates bilaterally.

prompt: Name the brainstem motor nuclei that receive corticobulbar input for voluntary head movement.
answer: Motor trigeminal, facial, nucleus ambiguus, hypoglossal

prompt: Which cranial motor nucleus controls the muscles of mastication?
answer: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve (CN V)

prompt: Which fiber bundle conveys voluntary motor signals from cortex to the facial nucleus?
Which fiber bundle conveys voluntary signals from cortex to the spinal accessory nucleus (shrugging)?
explain: The spinal accessory nucleus (CN XI) lies in the upper cervical spinal cord, not the brainstem, so it is reached by corticospinal fibers rather than corticobulbar fibers.

prompt: Where do corticobulbar axons cross relative to their target motor nucleus (as drawn in lab 10)?
answer: Just superior to the motor nucleus
explain: Corticobulbar axons descend uncrossed to the level of the target motor nucleus and then cross just above it, so the nucleus receives input from the opposite cortex (and, for most nuclei, also the same side).

prompt: Which nucleus controls muscles of speech and swallowing (CN IX, X)?
Which motor nucleus controls the tongue muscles?
A lesion of the right facial nucleus/nerve paralyses which part of the face?
answer: The entire right half of the face (ipsilateral, upper and lower)

prompt: Where do corticopontine fibers synapse?
answer: Ipsilateral pontine nuclei in the ventral (basilar) pons

prompt: Pontine nuclei axons cross and enter the cerebellum via which peduncle?
Corticopontocerebellar information reaches which cerebellar hemisphere relative to the cortex?
explain: Corticopontine fibers synapse in the ipsilateral pontine nuclei, whose axons cross in the transverse pontine fibers into the middle cerebellar peduncle, so each cerebellar hemisphere receives plan information from the opposite cerebral cortex.

prompt: About what fraction of cortical efferent fibers at the midbrain are corticopontine?
Where do rubrospinal neurons originate?
What movement does the rubrospinal tract promote?
answer: Flexion of the contralateral upper limb

prompt: In which funiculus does the rubrospinal tract descend?
answer: Lateral funiculus (next to the lateral corticospinal tract)

prompt: The red nucleus receives input from which structures of the cerebellum?
answer: Contralateral deep cerebellar nuclei via the superior cerebellar peduncle

prompt: Posturing with flexed arms (lesion above the red nucleus) is called what?
Posturing with extended arms (lesion below the red nucleus) is called what?
Where do tectospinal fibers arise?
answer: Superior and inferior colliculi (tectum of the midbrain)

prompt: What does the tectospinal tract do?
answer: Turns the head and neck toward visual and auditory stimuli

prompt: Tectospinal axons synapse on lower motor neurons at which spinal levels?
Where do reticulospinal fibers originate?
Which reticulospinal tract facilitates extensor muscles?
Which reticulospinal tract inhibits extensors and facilitates flexion?
Where does the vestibulospinal tract originate?
What is the function of the vestibulospinal tract?
answer: Maintains head and body posture and balance (righting)

prompt: The vestibulospinal tract synapses on lower motor neurons of which muscles?
Which brainstem descending tracts innervate axial muscles (anterior funiculus)?
explain: The medial (anterior funiculus) brainstem tracts, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and tectospinal, terminate on medial motor pools and so control axial and proximal muscles for posture and head position.

prompt: Which descending tracts innervate limb muscles (lateral funiculus)?
explain: The lateral funiculus tracts, the lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal, end on lateral motor pools in the ventral horn and so control distal limb muscles.

prompt: Which descending tracts arise from the cortex?
answer: Corticospinal (lateral/anterior) and corticobulbar; the rest arise in the brainstem
explain: Only the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts originate in the cerebral cortex; the rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts arise in brainstem nuclei, though they are influenced by cortex.

prompt: What does 'extrapyramidal' mean?
answer: All descending motor tracts that are not corticospinal (outside the pyramids)

prompt: Which retinal cells are the photoreceptors?
In lecture 11's scheme, which retinal neurons are first-order and which second-order?
answer: Bipolar cells first-order; retinal ganglion cells second-order
review_note: Lecture 11 labels bipolar cells first-order and ganglion cells second-order; photoreceptors are the receptors. Confirm convention.

prompt: Retinal ganglion cell axons form which structure?
Which retinal fibers cross in the optic chiasm?
answer: Nasal (medial) hemiretina fibers; temporal fibers do not cross

prompt: Fibers crossing in the optic chiasm carry which part of each eye's visual field?
List the visual pathway from eye to cortex.
answer: Optic nerve, optic chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiations, primary visual cortex
explain: The path is optic nerve, optic chiasm (nasal fibers cross), optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, optic radiations (via the internal capsule) and primary visual cortex around the calcarine fissure.

prompt: Which thalamic nucleus relays vision to cortex?
Where do optic radiations terminate?
The upper visual field is represented in which part of primary visual cortex?
explain: The visual image is inverted on the retina, so the upper visual field falls on the lower retina and is represented in the inferior bank of the calcarine fissure (the lingual gyrus), below the sulcus. The lower field is represented above.

prompt: Name the three main destinations of retinal ganglion cell axons.
answer: Hypothalamus (suprachiasmatic nucleus), lateral geniculate nucleus, midbrain (superior colliculus/pretectal nucleus)
explain: Retinal ganglion cells also project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian rhythms), the superior colliculus (reflexive eye and head movements) and the pretectal nucleus (pupillary light reflex), in addition to the LGN for conscious vision.

prompt: Which retinal projection modulates circadian rhythms?
answer: Retinohypothalamic projection to the suprachiasmatic nucleus

prompt: A lesion of the left optic nerve causes what deficit?
A lesion of the optic chiasm (e.g. pituitary tumor) causes what field defect?
answer: Tunnel vision: loss of peripheral (temporal) vision in each eye (bitemporal hemianopia)

prompt: A lesion of the right optic tract causes what field defect?
Damage to the left inferior visual cortex causes what deficit?
explain: The lower bank of the calcarine fissure receives the upper visual field of the opposite side, so damage there causes a contralateral upper quadrantanopia (left lesion, right upper quadrant).

prompt: A left primary visual cortex lesion causes what deficit?
Which cortical stream identifies objects (the 'what' pathway) and where does it project?
answer: Ventral stream to the inferior temporal lobe

prompt: Which stream processes spatial vision and visually guided movement?
answer: Dorsal ('where') stream to the parietal lobe

prompt: Which cranial nerve is the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
Which cranial nerve and nucleus form the efferent limb of the pupillary light reflex?
answer: CN III from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus (parasympathetic)

prompt: Light in one eye causes constriction of which pupils?
explain: The pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, so light in one eye constricts both pupils: the same-side pupil is the direct response, the opposite one the consensual response.

prompt: Which midbrain area receives the optic input for the pupillary light reflex?
Which nerve is the afferent limb of the corneal blink reflex?
Which nerve and nucleus form the efferent limb of the corneal reflex?
Touching the left cornea closes which eyelids?
explain: Trigeminal input reaches both facial nuclei through the reticular formation, so the blink is bilateral: the stimulated eye closes (direct) and the opposite eye also closes (consensual).

prompt: Name the brainstem structures involved in the corneal blink reflex.
answer: CN V, spinal trigeminal nucleus, facial nucleus (CN VII)
explain: The afferent limb is the trigeminal nerve (V1) to the spinal trigeminal nucleus, interneurons connect to both facial nuclei, and the efferent limb is the facial nerve to orbicularis oculi.

prompt: Which cortical area drives voluntary horizontal saccades?
Right frontal eye field activation drives the eyes to which side, via which brainstem center?
answer: To the left, via the left PPRF (paramedian pontine reticular formation)

prompt: The PPRF activates which muscles for same-side gaze?
answer: Ipsilateral lateral rectus (abducens) and contralateral medial rectus (via MLF)

prompt: Which tract connects CN III, IV and VI nuclei for conjugate gaze?
A left MLF lesion in a patient asked to look right causes what finding?
answer: Left eye cannot adduct (medial rectus), right eye abducts; convergence intact

prompt: In the vestibulo-ocular reflex, turning the head right turns the eyes which way?
explain: The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes equal and opposite to head rotation so the image stays stable on the retina; a head turn to the right drives the eyes left.

prompt: Which midbrain structure mediates involuntary (reflexive) saccades?
Trace the auditory pathway from cochlear nerve to cortex.
answer: Cochlear nerve, cochlear nuclei (rostral medulla), inferior colliculus, medial geniculate nucleus, primary auditory cortex
explain: Cochlear nerve fibers synapse in the cochlear nuclei (rostral medulla), then the pathway is mostly bilateral through the superior olive and lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus, medial geniculate nucleus and primary auditory cortex.

prompt: Where are the cell bodies of the cochlear nerve?
Where do vestibular nerve fibers synapse in the brainstem?
answer: Vestibular nuclei (and directly into the cerebellum)
